stem: Who founded the Gaza state?

options.content: Soshangane, a general of Zwide
options.rationale: Correct: he fled north after the Ndwandwe were defeated.

options.content: Mzilikazi, a general of Shaka
options.rationale: Mzilikazi founded the Ndebele state.

options.content: Ngungunyana, the last king
options.rationale: Ngungunyana ruled from about 1884, long after the founding.

options.content: Changamire Dombo, the Rozvi leader
options.rationale: Dombo founded the Rozvi state in the seventeenth century.

explanation: Soshangane founded the Gaza state in the 1820s. Ngungunyana was the last important king.

stem: Which peoples were the main tributaries of the Gaza state?

options.content: The Tsonga, Chopi and Ndau peoples
options.rationale: Correct: conquered peoples of southern Mozambique and south-east Zimbabwe.

options.content: The Zulu, Swazi and Basotho peoples
options.rationale: These peoples had their own kingdoms in the south.

options.content: The Rozvi, Torwa and Mutapa
options.rationale: These were Shona-speaking states of the plateau.

options.content: The Herero, Nama and Ovambo
options.rationale: These peoples live in what is now Namibia.

explanation: The Gaza state ruled and taxed the Tsonga, Chopi and Ndau peoples.

stem: Why did many Gaza men work in South African mines in the 1880s?

options.content: To escape forced labour for the Gaza king
options.rationale: Work in the mines was not a flight from the king.

options.content: To earn wages that paid for guns and cloth
options.rationale: Correct: wages helped the state to arm itself.

options.content: To repay a tax owed to the Boer republic
options.rationale: They were not paying a Boer tax.

options.content: To join the army of the British Company
options.rationale: The Company did not recruit Gaza men for its army.

explanation: Migrant labour produced wages for guns and goods, linking Gaza to the new economy of southern Africa.

stem: What happened at Coolela on 7 November 1895?

options.content: The Gaza army defeated a Portuguese column
options.rationale: The Gaza army was defeated.

options.content: Ngungunyana signed a treaty with the British
options.rationale: No treaty was signed at Coolela.

options.content: A Portuguese force defeated the Gaza army
options.rationale: Correct: modern rifles and machine guns beat the regiments.

options.content: The Gaza state split into two kingdoms
options.rationale: The state ended when its king was captured.

explanation: At Coolela Portuguese firepower defeated the Gaza regiments, and Ngungunyana was captured at Chaimite on 28 December 1895.

stem: Why did the Portuguese decide to attack the Gaza state in 1895?

options.content: To free the Gaza people from the Boers for good
options.rationale: Boers did not rule the Gaza people.

options.content: To protect a Gaza king who asked for help
options.rationale: Ngungunyana was an enemy in 1895.

options.content: To get the Gaza army for service in Portugal
options.rationale: The Portuguese did not wish to recruit it.

options.content: To prove occupation and block Britain
options.rationale: Correct: after the Berlin Conference they needed to occupy their claims.

explanation: Portugal wished to confirm its claim against British and Boer ambitions, and its new weapons made a campaign possible.
hints: Recall the Scramble for Africa and the rule of effective occupation.

stem: Which factor best explains why Ngungunyana could not unite his subjects against Portugal?

options.content: All of his subjects were forbidden to own any shields
options.rationale: There was no such rule.

options.content: Portugal had already conquered the Tsonga in 1850
options.rationale: Portuguese power was weak until the 1890s.

options.content: Tributaries resented Gaza rule and helped Portugal
options.rationale: Correct: internal divisions weakened the resistance.

options.content: His regiments refused to fight because of plague
options.rationale: No such refusal is recorded.

explanation: Resentment among tributaries and divisions within the Gaza leadership meant that Ngungunyana could not unite all his subjects.
hints: Think about how the conquered peoples regarded Gaza rule.

stem: Which comparison of the Gaza and Ndebele states is accurate?

options.content: Both were conquered by Portugal in one campaign
options.rationale: The Ndebele were conquered by the British South Africa Company.

options.content: Both were founded by generals who served under Shaka
options.rationale: Soshangane had served under Zwide.

options.content: Both ruled the whole plateau of present-day Zimbabwe
options.rationale: Neither ruled the whole plateau.

options.content: Both were Nguni states with regiments, ended by Europeans
options.rationale: Correct: the Ndebele fell in 1893-94 and Gaza in 1895.

explanation: Both were Nguni states with regiments; the Ndebele fell to the Company in 1893-94 and Gaza to the Portuguese in 1895.
hints: Check each statement for the founder and the conqueror.

stem: The Gaza state took its name from Soshangane's grandfather, Gasa.
explanation: True. The name Gaza comes from the ancestor Gasa.

stem: For most of the nineteenth century the Portuguese were strong enough to control the Gaza kings.
explanation: False. The Portuguese were weak in the interior and often had to pay or please the Gaza kings.

stem: Ngungunyana tried to protect his independence by playing the Portuguese and the British against each other.
explanation: True. He sought British protection while dealing with the Portuguese, but the policy failed.
hints: Recall his messages to the British.

stem: Describe the political organisation of the Gaza state.

points.description: A king (inkosi) held supreme power
Izinduna advised and governed for him
Conquered peoples (Tsonga, Chopi, Ndau) paid tribute through appointed officials or chiefs
Age regiments served as the army

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The king held supreme power and was helped by izinduna who advised and governed for him. Conquered peoples such as the Tsonga, Chopi and Ndau were ruled through appointed officials or chiefs and paid tribute. The state's army was organised in age regiments.

explanation: One mark for each feature.

stem: Explain why the Gaza kings were able to dominate the Portuguese for most of the nineteenth century.

points.description: The Gaza army was large and well organised and the Portuguese had only small forts on the coast and in the valleys
The Portuguese depended on the Gaza king's goodwill for trade and often paid tribute to keep their posts

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Gaza army was large and well organised, while the Portuguese had only small forts and few soldiers in the interior. They also depended on the king's goodwill for trade and often paid tribute to keep their posts.

explanation: One mark for each point and one for developing it.
hints: Compare the forces and the interests of each side.

stem: Explain **two** reasons for the fall of the Gaza state in 1895.

points.description: The Portuguese had modern rifles and machine guns that defeated the regiments
Internal divisions and discontented tributaries weakened the state, and some helped the Portuguese

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Portuguese brought modern rifles and machine guns, which defeated the Gaza regiments at Coolela. The state was also weakened by divisions in the royal family and by discontented tributary peoples, some of whom helped the Portuguese.

explanation: One mark for each reason and one for explaining it.
hints: One reason is about weapons, one about unity.

points.description: Portuguese rifles and machine guns won at Coolela and the capture of Ngungunyana ended the state
But Portugal acted only after 1885 for international reasons, and internal weaknesses (tributaries, divided family) made the conquest easier

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Portuguese military power was the immediate cause, since modern rifles and machine guns defeated the regiments at Coolela and the capture of Ngungunyana ended the state. But the Portuguese were weak for most of the century and acted only after the Berlin Conference, when they needed to prove effective occupation. The state's internal weaknesses, such as discontented tributaries and divisions in the royal family, made the conquest easier. I conclude that military power was decisive, but it succeeded because of international pressures and internal weakness.

explanation: Credit both sets of reasons and a supported judgement.
hints: Consider weapons first, then political conditions.

Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a report by a fictional Portuguese officer after a battle in 1895 (invented for this question)

> The enemy came on in great numbers, brave and well disciplined, but they had no answer to our rifles and our machine guns. Many were killed before they came within reach of our line. The people of the neighbouring districts, who have long suffered from the king's demands for tribute, did not come to his help.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The two sources can be trusted on some points but not all. Source A is a report by a Portuguese officer after victory, so he may exaggerate the strength of his weapons and emphasise the king's harsh rule to justify the conquest. Source B was told long afterwards by a member of a tributary people and may reflect resentment of the Gaza rulers. However, the two sources come from opposite sides and agree that the tributary peoples did not help the king, which my own knowledge of discontent over tribute supports. Neither explains the international reasons for the Portuguese campaign, so they are reliable on internal division but incomplete as a whole.

explanation: Both sources are invented: a victor's report and a tradition from a conquered people.
hints: For (c), consider who wrote each source and when, then use your own knowledge.

stem: Compare the Gaza state with the Ndebele state in their origins and organisation.

points.description: Similarities: founded by Nguni generals who fled the Zulu wars (Soshangane, Mzilikazi); age regiments; kings with izinduna; tribute from conquered peoples; cattle
Differences: Gaza in southern Mozambique and south-east Zimbabwe over Tsonga, Chopi and Ndau; Ndebele in south-west Zimbabwe over Shona, Sotho, Tswana
Differences in outside relations: Gaza dealt with Portugal and migrant labour; Ndebele with traders, concession seekers and the British South Africa Company
Judgement: broadly similar in organisation but different in setting and end

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Gaza and Ndebele states were similar in origin and organisation. Both were founded by Nguni generals, Soshangane and Mzilikazi, who fled the Zulu wars; both were ruled by kings with izinduna, relied on age regiments, took tribute from conquered peoples and valued cattle. They differed in setting: Gaza lay in southern Mozambique and the south-east of Zimbabwe and ruled the Tsonga, Chopi and Ndau, while the Ndebele settled in the south-west and ruled Shona, Sotho and Tswana people. Their foreign relations also differed: the Gaza dealt with the Portuguese and sent men to the South African mines, while the Ndebele dealt with traders, concession seekers and the British South Africa Company. They were therefore broadly similar kinds of state, shaped by different settings, and each was ended by a different European power.

explanation: Credit specific similarities and differences and a judgement.
hints: Give similarities, then differences, then a short judgement.
